To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) children’s stress symptoms are related to the level of stress experienced by parents, (2) children’s stress is related to parents’ involvement in coping activities, and (3) children’s stress in the face of ongoing terror is more related to parents’ stress and less related to parents’ coping activities when terror attacks are experienced in the parents’ city than when they are experienced elsewhere in the country.

(1) children of parents who live in a city that has experienced a terrorist attack are more likely to show stress symptoms and to be less involved in proactive coping activities; (2) adults who live in a community that has experienced a terror attack are not more likely to show symptoms of stress; (3) adults who live under the threat of terror, whether in an area with or without local terror attacks, are more likely to engage in proactive coping activities.
